title: Customer account takeover on a fictional retail banking portal
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional retail bank offers browser and mobile account access. Customers authenticate with username and password; optional SMS one-time codes are available but not required. Transaction history and payment initiation are available after login. Failed-login lockout occurs after many attempts. Logs record IP address, timestamp, and HTTP status only.
assumptions: MFA is optional and not enforced for all transactions.
Attackers can obtain breached credential lists from prior unrelated breaches.
No bot-management challenge is enforced on the login endpoint.

nodes.label: Take over a customer bank account
Automated credential stuffing using breached username/password pairs
Low-rate password spraying against known email usernames
Steal an authenticated user session
Phishing page capturing credentials and one-time code
Session fixation after insecure session handling
Account recovery flow bypass using weak challenge questions

mitigations: Require phishing-resistant MFA for login and payment initiation.
Enforce per-account and per-IP throttling with adaptive bot detection.
Bind sessions to device context and rotate session identifiers after authentication.
Remove security questions and use verified recovery channels.
Add anomaly detection for impossible travel and new device access.
uncertainty: The scenario does not specify whether credential stuffing controls already exist.
Impact depends on transaction limits and fraud reimbursement policy.
The model cannot verify the bank's actual control configuration from this description.

title: Privilege escalation in a fictional SaaS administration console
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional SaaS application has standard users, workspace administrators, and a super-admin role. Role checks are performed in the web API and a background job service. A self-service password reset sends a link to the user's email. Audit logs are retained for 30 days. The product exposes a documented REST API with API keys per workspace.
assumptions: At least one workspace has a compromised email account.
Role checks are assumed consistent but not independently verified.
API keys can be created by workspace administrators.

nodes.label: Gain super-admin or cross-workspace access
Hijack self-service password reset via compromised email inbox
Access another workspace through object-level authorization flaw
Use a leaked or over-scoped workspace API key for data export
Abuse a legitimate account to escalate roles
Phish a workspace administrator credential
Enroll MFA on a stolen account using weak verification

mitigations: Enforce MFA for all administrative actions and API key creation.
Add centralized authorization tests for object and workspace boundaries.
Shorten API key lifetime and support scoped, rotatable keys.
Add immutable audit logging with tamper-evident export.
Review reset flows for email account compromise scenarios.
uncertainty: The scenario does not state whether password reset links are single-use or time-limited.
Actual exploitability depends on API authorization implementation details not described.
No external CVE is asserted because this is a synthetic application design.

title: Unauthorized data access in a fictional healthcare scheduling API
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional clinic scheduling API lets reception staff search patients by name or date of birth. The API supports filtering by clinic ID. Authenticated users receive bearer tokens valid for 8 hours. Detailed appointment notes are returned in the same response as appointment metadata. An internal export endpoint supports CSV generation for reporting.
assumptions: At least one low-privilege reception account can be provisioned.
The export endpoint is reachable from the same network as the public API.
Query filters are constructed server-side but not yet independently tested.

nodes.label: Exfiltrate patient scheduling and note data
Manipulate object identifiers to read other patients' appointments
Use crafted filter values to widen search beyond assigned clinic
Steal and reuse a bearer token
Cross-site script execution in an admin-facing dashboard steals token
Bearer token exposed in diagnostic logs or browser storage
Abuse CSV export to collect larger data sets than the UI allows

mitigations: Enforce object-level authorization on every appointment and note field.
Minimize response payloads and separate note access behind additional authorization.
Apply allowlisted filter construction and test boundary cases.
Protect export endpoints with stronger authorization, pagination limits, and audit events.
Reduce token lifetime and avoid storing tokens in browser-accessible storage.
uncertainty: Impact assumes appointment notes contain sensitive clinical text; the scenario does not define note content.
The actual query implementation is unknown, so filter bypass is a plausible rather than confirmed risk.
This example is synthetic and not based on a real clinic system.

title: Supply-chain compromise of a fictional internal build pipeline
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional engineering team builds container images in an automated pipeline. Source dependencies are resolved from public package indexes and a private internal index. Build scripts run with credentials that can push images to a registry. Test artifacts are stored in the same registry namespace as production images. Developers can add build steps through pull requests subject to review. No dependency lockfile is currently enforced.
assumptions: An attacker can publish a package name that resembles an internal dependency.
Build logs may be visible to all authenticated developers.
Production deployment trusts registry image tags rather than digests.

nodes.label: Inject malicious code into a production container image
Dependency confusion causing installation of an attacker-controlled package
Typosquatted public package pulled by a missing internal package
Introduce a malicious build step through an approved but insufficiently reviewed pull request
Steal build or registry credentials from pipeline components
Secret printed in build logs and exposed to developers
Poison a shared build cache to alter compiled output
Overwrite a mutable production image tag after build approval

mitigations: Use a single private dependency index with explicit upstream mirrors and allowlists.
Enforce lockfiles and package hash verification in builds.
Replace mutable tags with immutable image digests in deployment manifests.
Scope build credentials with least privilege and workload identity.
Require two-reviewer approval for build and dependency configuration changes.
Separate test and production registry permissions and namespaces.
uncertainty: The scenario assumes deployment trusts tags; digest pinning is listed as a mitigation, not a verified current control.
Build review quality is unknown, so pull-request compromise remains plausible.
This is a synthetic example and does not identify a real vulnerable product.

title: Unauthorized smart-camera access in a fictional home-security deployment
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional vendor provides internet-connected cameras for small businesses. Devices arrive with a default administrator password. Remote management is exposed through a cloud relay. Firmware updates are signed, but update checks can be disabled by users. Camera streams are available through a mobile app using shared household accounts. Device logs are stored locally and not centrally reviewed.
assumptions: At least one device was installed without changing the default password.
Household accounts are shared among multiple people.
The cloud relay authenticates devices but not individual viewers.

nodes.label: View or download camera footage without authorization
Log in with factory-default credentials after deployment
Access streams through a shared household account with weak password
Abuse device pairing flow to add an unauthorized viewer
Compromise device firmware or management channel
Keep vulnerable firmware by disabling update checks
Exploit misconfigured relay authorization to reach device stream
Reach camera management from an untrusted local network

mitigations: Require unique per-device credentials and forced first-run password change.
Provide individual user accounts with revocation and audit events.
Disable local management exposure by default and require authenticated pairing.
Make security updates automatic and monitor disabled update states.
Segment devices on isolated networks and review local logs centrally.
uncertainty: The scenario does not specify actual firmware vulnerability status; firmware attack paths are plausible.
Impact depends on deployment type and whether recording is enabled.
This vendor and product are fictional.

title: Remote access abuse in a fictional hybrid VPN deployment
task: Generate a reviewed-style attack tree from a system description
system: A fictional company uses a VPN to provide remote access to internal dashboards and file shares. MFA is required at login but not on every connection. Session tokens are valid for 24 hours. Split tunneling allows direct internet access while connected. Some file shares grant broad group access. VPN logs include connection and byte counts only; no endpoint posture checks are performed.
assumptions: Attackers can target employees with phishing.
At least one endpoint is unmanaged or outdated.
VPN group memberships include excessive file-share permissions.

nodes.label: Gain unauthorized access to internal resources through the VPN
MFA fatigue prompting an employee to approve an attacker's login
Steal or replay a 24-hour VPN session token
Use an employee's compromised device to connect over the VPN
Expand access from the VPN into broad internal data stores
Access over-permissioned file shares through default group membership
Use split tunneling to mix untrusted and trusted traffic during remote work
Connect from an unmanaged or outdated endpoint because no posture check exists

mitigations: Use phishing-resistant MFA and transaction-specific authorization for sensitive actions.
Shorten VPN session lifetime and bind sessions to device posture.
Disable split tunneling or enforce DNS and traffic controls for remote access.
Apply least privilege and periodic access reviews to file-share groups.
Add endpoint health checks and quarantine for noncompliant devices.
Enrich VPN logs with device identity and destination access context.
uncertainty: The scenario does not state whether VPN traffic is inspected after connection.
Actual lateral movement depends on internal segmentation not described.
This example is synthetic and not tied to a real company.
